Separation of Mixtures Take about a half test tubeful of bench hydrochloric acid in a clean porcelain basin.
Add about a half test tubeful of bench sodium hydroxide a little ate time with the help of a glass tube.
Stir the mixture constantly with a glass rod.
Introduce the mixture solution on the pieces of both red and blue litmus paper with the help of a glass rod.
If blue litmus paper turns red then the mixture solution is acidic.
Then, add few drops of bench NaOH with the help of the glass tube.
Stir the solution. Introduce the same solution on the piece of blue litmus paper again.
If the blue litmus paper is not affected, introduce the solution on the piece of red litmus paper.
If the red litmus paper turns blue, add few drops of bench HCl. Stir the solution.
Introduce the same solution on the piece of blue litmus paper. If the litmus paper is not affected, the solution is neutral.
If the blue litmus turns red, the alkali is introduced dropwise.
Similarly, if the red litmus turns blue, the acid is introduced dropwise. In this way, the neutral point is ascertained (obtained) by trial and error method.
When the mixture solution does not change the colours of both types of litmus papers, the solution is neutral.
Filter the solution and evaporate it to dryness to get solid sodium chloride.
Take a pinch of the common salt in a test tube. Dissolve it in water.
Add few drops of silver nitrate solution to it. Appearance of a curdy white precipitate indicates the presence of chloride salt.

RESULT
Common salt was obtained by neutralisation of bench HCl by bench NaOH followed by evaporation.
PRECAUTIONS
1. The mixture solution should be completely neutral.
2. All the glasswares should be handled with care.
3. Separate glass tubes should be used for acid and base bottles.

THEORY

Fractional crystallisation is the method employed to separate the components of a mixture of two or more soluble solids having different solubility. When a solution containing dissolved crystalline solids with varying solubility is gradually crystallised, the solid with lower solubility (here, potassium nitrate) is crystallised out first. Another solid (here, cupric nitrate) remains in the mother liquor which is crystallised out later.
Crystallisation can be defined as the process of getång the crystals of pure solid when a saturated solution of the solid is evaporated to a temperature, called crystallisation point and then cooled.
